title: Uthai Thani–Nakhon Sawan 2-Day Trip, Thailand | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 2-day, 1-night Uthai Thani to Nakhon Sawan itinerary in central Thailand: two riverside towns just 45 minutes apart. Wat Tha Sung, Khao Sakae Krang, Trok Rong Ya old town, the Chao Phraya River source at Pasan, and Bueng Boraphet — with timings, food, and where to stay.

h1:
Uthai Thani–Nakhon Sawan
2 Days, 1 Night Across Two Provinces
intro: Uthai Thani and Nakhon Sawan are two neighboring riverside towns only about 45 minutes apart by car. Most people visit them one at a time, but they pair into a single trip easily. One is a small, quiet town on the Sakae Krang River; the other is where four rivers meet to form the Chao Phraya. This plan runs 2 days and 1 night, starting in Uthai Thani before crossing over to Nakhon Sawan, with an easy pace and riverside food breaks along the way.

blocks.html: The nice thing about pairing Uthai Thani with Nakhon Sawan is how short the hop is. From downtown Uthai Thani to downtown Nakhon Sawan is around 50 kilometers, roughly a 45-minute to one-hour drive on easy highway — no rough roads to deal with. Both are river towns too: Uthai Thani sits on the Sakae Krang River, while Nakhon Sawan is the point where the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers converge into the Chao Phraya. So you get a riverside feel across both days.

This trip works best with your own car, since several sights in both towns sit just outside the center and cross-province public transport isn't very convenient. If you don't have a car, you can take a bus or van to Nakhon Sawan (the bigger hub) and then pick up a rental or taxi into Uthai Thani. The plan below starts with Uthai Thani because it's the smaller, quieter town — good for a slow first night — and closes in Nakhon Sawan, which has more food and photo spots.

items: Distance between towns — downtown Uthai Thani ↔ downtown Nakhon Sawan, about 50 km, a 45–60 min drive
Best season — November to February, cool and comfortable; in the late-rain, early-cool window the water in Bueng Boraphet and the rivers is full and the views are at their best
Overnight — we suggest spending the one night in Uthai Thani (there are riverside raft houses on the Sakae Krang and small in-town stays with good atmosphere)
Rough budget — lodging 700–1,500 THB/night + around 300–500 THB/person per day for food + fuel

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Uthai Thani — a small town on the Sakae Krang River

items.note: Start the day at the riverside morning market in town — a real slice of local Uthai life with traditional breakfast options like noodles, old-style coffee, and Chinese doughnuts (pa thong ko). Just walk and graze.

items.activity: Khao Sakae Krang–Wat Sangkat Rattana Khiri
items.note: Head up Khao Sakae Krang to pay respects and take in 360-degree views of Uthai town and the Sakae Krang River. There are 449 steps, or you can drive to the top. Go in the morning while the sun is still soft and the walk is easy.

About 12 km from town. The highlight is the Glass Temple (Wihan Kaeo), with mosaic-tiled walls that shimmer from end to end. This is Luang Pho Ruesi Ling Dam's temple — large, with plenty to wander. Dress modestly.
Head back into town and find a restaurant on the Sakae Krang River. Try the river fish or the noodles Uthai Thani is known for.
Stroll the Trok Rong Ya old quarter — old wooden buildings, coffee shops, snacks, and wall murals, with a retro feel. An easy late-afternoon walk for photos.

items.activity: Check in at a raft house/riverside stay + sunset
items.note: Check in, relax, and watch the sunset over the Sakae Krang River. The town goes quiet in the evening — perfect for sitting by the water.

blocks.title: Day 1 tip
blocks.html: The Uthai Thani morning market is busiest before 8 a.m. — if you sleep in, some food starts to sell out. To catch the full atmosphere, go a little early. And since Wat Tha Sung covers a lot of ground, wear comfortable walking shoes.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Crossing to Nakhon Sawan — the source of the Chao Phraya

items.activity: Leave Uthai Thani, head for Nakhon Sawan
items.note: Pack up, grab a light breakfast, and drive out of town. It takes about 45–60 minutes to reach downtown Nakhon Sawan (Pak Nam Pho).

items.activity: Pasan–source of the Chao Phraya River
items.note: The landmark marking the source of the Chao Phraya, where four rivers meet. The Pasan structure has a graceful curved design, and there are riverside cafes where you can sip coffee and watch the two-toned water.

items.activity: Pak Nam Pho noodles for lunch
items.note: Pak Nam Pho is known for its noodles and egg noodles. Several old-school shops sit around the market — try the marinated pork egg noodles or a traditional bowl of noodles.

Thailand's largest freshwater lake, with an aquarium building and a fish tunnel where you can see over 100 freshwater species. In the late-rain, early-cool season there are plenty of birds, and you can take a boat out on the lake.
A tower about as tall as a 10-story building, with a lift to the top for views over Pak Nam Pho, Khao Kop, and Bueng Boraphet from up high. The evening light is lovely.

items.activity: Dechatiwong Bridge, the two-toned river view
items.note: Finish at the riverside viewpoint on the Chao Phraya, watching the sunset and the different colors of the converging rivers before you head home.

blocks.text: Food you shouldn't miss in either town

blocks.html: Both are river towns, so the food revolves around river fish, noodles, and morning-market fare. Try working through this list over the course of the trip.

items.name: Pak Nam Pho noodles/egg noodles (Nakhon Sawan)
items.blurb: The signature dish of Pak Nam Pho. Several old shops around the market serve marinated pork egg noodles and traditional noodles that locals have eaten for generations.

items.name: Sakae Krang river fish (Uthai Thani)
items.blurb: Several riverside restaurants in downtown Uthai Thani serve river-fish dishes — grilled, fried, in curry — homestyle and full-flavored, eaten with a riverside view.

items.name: Uthai Thani riverside morning-market food
items.blurb: The Sakae Krang morning market has the full local lineup — old-style coffee, Chinese doughnuts, noodles, Thai sweets — to graze through in the morning.

items.name: Pasan riverside cafe (Nakhon Sawan)
items.blurb: At the source of the Chao Phraya there are riverside cafes for a coffee while you watch the two-toned water — a good stop in the late morning or afternoon of day two.

items.name: Old-style coffee & snacks at Trok Rong Ya (Uthai Thani)
items.blurb: The Trok Rong Ya old quarter has retro coffee shops and snacks to drop into, set among old wooden buildings — a good afternoon break.

blocks.html: For this trip we suggest spending the first night in Uthai Thani — the town is small and quiet, with good-atmosphere stays on the Sakae Krang River, both raft houses and small in-town hotels, and it's an easy walk to the riverside market in the morning. If you'd rather stay on the Nakhon Sawan side, downtown Pak Nam Pho has more hotels to choose from and sits closer to the food. Pick whichever suits your trip.

items.name: Sakae Krang riverside stays, Uthai Thani
items.blurb: Riverside raft houses and small in-town hotels — quiet, within walking distance of the morning market, good for the first night.

items.name: Pak Nam Pho hotels, Nakhon Sawan
items.blurb: More lodging options, close to the food and central sights — a good choice if you'd rather finish on the Nakhon Sawan side.

blocks.title: Can be done in one day
blocks.html: With only a day, pick half the highlights from each — say, a morning at the riverside market and Khao Sakae Krang in Uthai Thani, then an afternoon crossing to Pasan and Bueng Boraphet in Nakhon Sawan. That covers both towns in a tighter loop.

faq.q: How far apart are Uthai Thani and Nakhon Sawan, and is it a long drive?
faq.a: From downtown Uthai Thani to downtown Nakhon Sawan is around 50 kilometers, roughly a 45-minute to one-hour drive on easy highway. It fits nicely to pair the two towns into a 2-day, 1-night trip.

faq.q: Which town should I visit first?
faq.a: We suggest starting in Uthai Thani, since it's the smaller, quieter town and suits a slow first night, then crossing over to finish in Nakhon Sawan, which has more food and photo spots. You can flip the order to match wherever you start from, though.

faq.q: Can I do this trip without my own car?
faq.a: You can, but it's less convenient, since several sights sit outside the town centers. The easiest way is to take a bus or van to Nakhon Sawan, the bigger hub, then rent a car or use taxis from there. Having your own car is the most flexible option.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit?
faq.a: November to February, when the weather is cool and comfortable — the late-rain, early-cool window when the water in Bueng Boraphet and the rivers is full. The riverside views and the birds at Bueng Boraphet are at their best then.

faq.q: Where exactly is the source of the Chao Phraya in Nakhon Sawan?
faq.a: It's at Pasan in the Pak Nam Pho area, the point where the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers converge into the Chao Phraya. The Pasan structure is the landmark, with riverside cafes where you can sit and watch the two-toned water.
